summary: Morocco grants visa-free entry for up to 90 days to a long list of nationalities — including the US, UK, EU, Canada, Australia, Japan, Brazil, Mexico, Russia and China — and runs an official eVisa system (acces-maroc.ma) for several other nationalities; the dirham is a closed currency, so bring foreign cash or cards and change money inside the country.

conditionalWaivers.text: Visa-required nationals holding a valid multiple-entry sticker visa (90+ days remaining) from the US, Schengen, the UK, Ireland, Canada, Australia, Japan, Norway or New Zealand qualify for Morocco's eVisa (electronic authorisations like ESTA do not count).

source.name: Accès Maroc — official Morocco eVisa portal

fee.notes: Approximate standard fee (roughly 70–80 USD); an express 24-hour track costs more. The exact amount is shown on the official portal before payment.

source.name: Morocco Official Electronic Visa Portal (Accès Maroc)

fee.notes: Approximate. Fees vary by nationality and number of entries; the consulate quotes the exact amount in local currency.

source.name: Moroccan MFA Consular Portal

passportValidity.text: Your passport must be valid for the full duration of your stay in Morocco; at least 6 months' validity on arrival is recommended, and some airlines apply the stricter standard at check-in.

source.name: Moroccan MFA Consular Portal
Moroccan MFA Consular Portal

travelInsurance.text: Travel insurance is not an entry requirement for tourists, but medical coverage is recommended — private clinics expect payment up front and serious cases may need evacuation to Europe.

source.name: Moroccan MFA Consular Portal

onwardTicket.text: Onward travel is not systematically checked, but border officers and airlines may ask for proof of return or onward travel and an address in Morocco (the arrival form asks for one).

source.name: Moroccan MFA Consular Portal

proofOfFunds.text: There is no published fixed amount, but border officers may ask travelers to show sufficient means of support for the intended stay.

source.name: Moroccan MFA Consular Portal

currencyLimits.text: The Moroccan dirham (MAD) is a closed currency: you may bring in or take out at most 1,000 MAD. Foreign currency can be imported freely but amounts of 100,000 MAD equivalent or more must be declared; keep exchange receipts to convert leftover dirhams back before departure.

source.name: Moroccan Customs Administration (ADII)

notes: Drones may not be brought into Morocco without prior authorization — undeclared drones are confiscated at the airport.
Duty-free allowance: 200 cigarettes and 1 liter of spirits per adult.
Exporting significant quantities of antiques, fossils or cultural artefacts requires a permit.

payments.text: Cards are accepted in hotels, riads and modern restaurants in the cities, but souks, taxis, mountain villages and most small businesses are cash-only. Change money at banks or official bureaux inside Morocco. The dirham cannot legally be bought abroad.

safety.text: Morocco is generally safe for visitors with a strong tourist-police presence in the main cities. The most common problems are pickpocketing, aggressive touts and "faux guides" in the medinas of Marrakech and Fes — be polite but firm, and agree taxi and guide prices in advance.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Morocco travel advice

bestTimeToVisit.text: March to May and September to November offer warm days and cool nights — ideal for the imperial cities, the Atlas Mountains and the desert. Mid-summer is very hot inland; coastal cities like Essaouira stay pleasant.

idp.text: Morocco is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either.

driving.text: Morocco is a party to both the 1949 Geneva and the 1968 Vienna Conventions on Road Traffic, so it recognizes an International Driving Permit issued under either. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Morocco yet.

tips.text: The dirham is a closed currency. You may carry at most 1,000 MAD in or out of Morocco. Change money inside the country and convert leftovers back (keep exchange receipts) before you leave.

In Marrakech and Fes medinas, decline unsolicited "guides" and directions — helpers expect payment and often lead you to commission-paying shops. Hire licensed guides through your riad or the tourist office.
Bringing a drone into Morocco without prior authorization is prohibited — customs confiscate them on arrival, and getting one back on departure is slow and not guaranteed.

During Ramadan many cafés and restaurants close in the daytime and opening hours shrink; eating, drinking or smoking in public during fasting hours is disrespectful (and prosecutable for Muslims). Tourist hotels serve meals as usual.

faq.question: Do US citizens need a visa for Morocco?
faq.answer: No. US passport holders can visit Morocco visa-free for up to 90 days. Your passport is stamped on entry. Check the stamp, as staying beyond 90 days without an extension from the police is an offense.

faq.question: How long can EU and UK citizens stay in Morocco?
faq.answer: Citizens of the UK and all EU countries can stay visa-free for up to 90 days. For longer stays you must apply for an extension at a local police station well before the 90 days expire, or leave and re-enter, though frequent back-to-back runs can be refused.

faq.question: Can I buy Moroccan dirhams before my trip?
faq.answer: Effectively no. The dirham is a closed currency and importing or exporting more than 1,000 MAD is prohibited. Bring euros, dollars or pounds (or use ATMs) and change money at banks or official exchange bureaux in Morocco. Keep receipts so you can convert leftover dirhams back before departure.

faq.question: Who needs Morocco's eVisa and where do you apply?
faq.answer: Most Western, Latin American and East Asian passports do not need any visa. Nationalities that do — including India and several African and Asian countries — can check eligibility and apply at the official portal acces-maroc.ma; the eVisa is typically issued within about 3 business days (24 hours on the express track). Travelers not eligible online apply at a Moroccan embassy.

faq.question: Is tap water safe to drink in Morocco?
faq.answer: Tap water in the big cities is chlorinated but most visitors' stomachs are not used to it — bottled or filtered water is recommended everywhere, and essential in rural areas and the desert.
